JUSTICE ALITO, concurring in the judgment.
I agree with the Court that the Seventh Circuit used an erroneously low standard for determining whether the plaintiffs in this case
satisfied their burden of pleading * * *. I further agree that the case should be remanded to allow the lower courts to decide in the first
instance whether the allegations survive under the correct standard. In two respects, however, I disagree with the opinion of the Court.
First, the best interpretation of the statute is that only those facts that are alleged “with particularity” may properly be considered in
determining whether the allegations of scienter are sufficient. Second, I agree with Justice SCALIA that a “strong inference” of scienter,
in the present context, means an inference that is more likely than not correct.
NOTES AND QUESTIONS
1. The PSLRA includes two separate pleading requirements. As the Third Circuit has explained:
First, * * * the complaint “must specify each allegedly misleading statement, why the statement was misleading, and, if an allegation is
made on information and belief, all facts supporting that belief with particularity.” * * * Second, the complaint must, “with respect to each
act or omission alleged to violate this chapter, state with particularity facts giving rise to a strong inference that the defendant acted with the
required state of mind.”
Institutional Invs. Group v. Avaya, Inc., 564 F.3d 242, 252–53 (3d Cir. 2009) (quoting 15 U.S.C. § 78u–4(b)(1)–(2)). How does this dual approach
differ from the requirement of particularity under Rule 9(b)?
2.The relevant question under Tellabs is whether a reasonable person would think that the inference of scienter is cogent and compelling. Is it
significant that the Supreme Court used the word “would” and not “could”? Some commentary has argued that this word choice suggests “that even if a
reasonable person could conclude that the inference of scienter is sufficient, the complaint still fails if a reasonable person could also reach the opposite
conclusion.” See Miller, Pleading After Tellabs, 2009 Wis.L.Rev. 507, 510 (2009).
3.The Court in Tellabs appears to have assumed that pre-filing investigation suffices to enable a plaintiff to meet its pleading standard. See
Nelles & Huber, Pleading Securities Fraud Claims: The Good, The Bad, and The Ugly, 45 Loy.U.Chi.L.J. 653 (2014). If this assumption is wrong,
critics argue, then Tellabs does not simply weed out frivolous cases—as the PSLRA was intended to do—but rather “also weeds out cases where the
allegations of scienter are not strong, but where, with the benefit of discovery, the plaintiff might be able to establish the requisite state of mind at trial.”
Miller, A Modest Proposal for Securities Pleading After Tellabs, 7 L. & Contemp.Probs. 93, 102–03 (2012).
